topic: Time to analgesia in the emergency department

audits.title: Time to Analgesia- a Geriatric Emergency Medicine Audit in Patients Presenting with Head Injuries
audits.standard: RCEM: analgesia within 15 minutes of presentation
audits.setting: Emergency Department, St Vincent's University Hospital; patients aged 75 or over with head injury

cycle1.result: Average time from registration to analgesia just under 3 hours.

cycle2.result: Significant improvement in time to analgesia reported (no figures); final results awaited.

audits.other_findings: A significant proportion of older patients did not receive analgesia.
audits.citation: Gallagher O, O’Leary A. Time to Analgesia- a Geriatric Emergency Medicine Audit in Patients Presenting with Head Injuries. Age and Ageing. 2026;55(Supplement_2). doi:10.1093/ageing/afag197.034.

audits.title: An Australian audit of ED pain management patterns.
audits.standard: Timely and appropriate pain management as an ED quality indicator

cycle1.result: Triage pain score documented in 547 (56.4%); 1473 (74.9%) of those in pain received analgesia; 644 (32.7%) opioid; median time to analgesia 70 minutes (IQR 58 to 92).

audits.citation: Fry M, Bennetts S, Huckson S. An Australian audit of ED pain management patterns. J Emerg Nurs. 2011;37(3):269-274. doi:10.1016/j.jen.2010.03.007. PMID: 21550463.

audits.title: Time to analgesia for care delivered by nurse practitioners in the emergency department – a retrospective chart audit.
audits.standard: Timely analgesia (within 30 minutes) and pain score documentation
audits.setting: Emergency department, nurse practitioner service (The Alfred Hospital, Melbourne)

cycle1.result: Pain scores documented in 67 (52.3%); median time to analgesia 60.5 minutes; 34 (26.6%) received analgesia within 30 minutes of presentation; 65 (61.3%) within 30 minutes of NP assessment.

audits.other_findings: 22 (17.2%) received analgesia before nurse practitioner assessment; median time from assessment 25 minutes.
audits.citation: Jennings N, Kansal A, O'Reilly G, Mitra B, Gardner G. Time to analgesia for care delivered by nurse practitioners in the emergency department – a retrospective chart audit. Int Emerg Nurs. 2015;23(2):71-74. doi:10.1016/j.ienj.2014.07.002. PMID: 25113664.

audits.title: A multi-faceted approach to increase appropriate analgesia prescribing in the emergency department.
audits.standard: RCEM analgesia guidelines, including analgesia within 20 minutes for severe pain
audits.setting: Emergency department, tertiary hospital in London (St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust); abdominal pain patients

cycle1.result: Guideline-compliant analgesia 29%; pain score at triage 38%; rechecked 19%; severe pain treated within 20 minutes 22%

audits.intervention: Locally adapted RCEM guidelines, monthly doctor and nurse teaching, and a nurse prescriber champion

cycle2.result: Pain score at triage 87%; guideline-concordant analgesia 52%; severe pain acted on in time 40%

audits.other_findings: Cycle 3 (n=33) showed improvement returned to baseline without monthly education.
audits.citation: Ratneswaran C, Dodd K, Enright K, Dasan S. A multi-faceted approach to increase appropriate analgesia prescribing in the emergency department. BMJ Qual Improv Rep. 2015;4(1):u204091.w3774. doi:10.1136/bmjquality.u204091.w3774. PMID: 26734441.

audits.title: Improving door-to-analgesia timing in musculoskeletal injuries in an academic emergency department in India: a quality improvement project.
audits.standard: Aim to reduce time to first analgesia by 30% from baseline
audits.intervention: Pain score at triage, fast-tracking of moderate-severe pain, resident awareness sessions, pain management protocol and prescription audits.
audits.citation: Sadasivam S A, Kumaran A, Manu Ayyan S, Sindujaa SN. Improving door-to-analgesia timing in musculoskeletal injuries in an academic emergency department in India: a quality improvement project. BMJ Open Qual. 2024;13(2):e002815. doi:10.1136/bmjoq-2024-002815. PMID: 38834372.
